registrations.newExplanation: For somebody who asked in person, on the phone, or after a run. It enters exactly like a registration the participant made themselves: the same order for places, the same waiting list, the same starting state. They receive the ordinary confirmation email and sign the declaration themselves — nobody can sign one for somebody else.
registrations.noEventsAcceptingRegistrations: No event takes registrations through the platform. Set the registration mode to "Register here" on the event page.
registrations.participantEmailHelp: The confirmation and the declaration link go here. It must be their address, not the club's.
registrations.participantLocale: Language we write to them in
registrations.participantLocaleHelp: The language of every email about this registration.
registrations.listOptIn: The person wants to appear on the public participant list
registrations.relayConfirmation: I confirm this person asked me to register them.
registrations.correctNameHelp: Only the name can be corrected. The email address is the participant's identity and is never changed here: for a wrong address, cancel the registration and add it again with the right one.
registrations.cancelHelp: A registration is never deleted — it records what somebody agreed to and when. Cancelling releases the place, and it goes to the first person on the waiting list.
registrations.auditActorParticipant: the participant, from their own link

registration.confirmed_by_staff: Confirmed at the desk (address vouched for, declaration on paper)
registration.promoted_by_staff: Given a place ahead of the waiting list
registration.list_consent_changed: Public-list choice changed by the participant

registrations.deleteHelp: Deletes the registration and the signed declaration, permanently. The place is released to the waiting list, and the log keeps who deleted it and why — not the person’s data. Use it for an erasure request; for an ordinary withdrawal, cancel instead.
registrations.deleteConfirm: I confirm this deletion is permanent
registrations.tableCaption: Registrations, with status, step, event and date submitted
registrations.emptyFiltered: No registration matches these filters. Clear them to see all of them.
registrations.bulkCancelHelp: Each ticked registration is cancelled separately, with the same reason, and each place goes to the first person on the waiting list. Permanent erasure is never done in bulk.
registrations.registrationsCancelled: {cancelled} registrations cancelled. {failed} could not be cancelled.
registrations.searchHelp: Search by name, with or without Romanian diacritics.
registrations.resendQrLong: Send the confirmation again, with the QR code and the manage link
registrations.checkinCodeHelp: The code from the confirmation email; the QR below encodes it. Used at the number pickup desk.

journey.title: The registration's journey
journey.heldKept: deadline passed, the place is kept while nobody waits
journey.legend:
The six steps of a registration:
– 1 form submitted
– 2 email confirmed
– 3 place held
– 4 declaration signed
– 5 place confirmed
– 6 number collected at the desk
The figure says which one they have reached.

registrations.readOnlyNotice: You can read the list, the export and the race numbers, but nothing here changes a registration: cancelling, erasing, resending an email and the “bib printed” mark are the Administrator’s. On race day you can still confirm on a paper declaration, give a place, set a number and check somebody in — from “Race day”.
registrations.bibProvisional: Provisional number — it is settled when registration closes, and only then is it emailed.
registrations.bibSettled: The race number is {number} and is settled: the participant has been emailed it and it may already be printed.
registrations.bibHeldNow: Race number: {number} — provisional until registration closes.
registrations.bibsPrintedAlert: {count, plural, one {# bib marked as printed.} other {# bibs marked as printed.}}
registrations.bibsUnprintedAlert: {count, plural, one {# bib no longer marked as printed.} other {# bibs no longer marked as printed.}}
registrations.cancelBody: The place is released through the allocator and offered at once to the first person waiting. An audit row records who cancelled. It cannot be undone: if they change their mind, they register again.
registrations.confirmOnPaperBody: You are confirming that the participant signed the declaration on paper, at the desk. They get the place and a race number, and the audit row names you as the person who recorded the signature. Use it only with the signed paper in front of you.
registrations.eraseTypeNameHelp: Type “{name}” exactly, so we know this is the row you meant. Capitals and diacritics do not matter.
registrations.summaryScopeHelp: The numbers above are for the selected event alone; the figure on the Înscrieri tab counts every event still to come.
registrations.bulkEraseTitle: Erase the ticked registrations for good
registrations.bulkEraseHelp: They are removed, their places are released, and it cannot be undone. Only an audit line remains: who erased and why, never whom.
registrations.bulkEraseConfirm: Type how many you are erasing
registrations.bulkEraseConfirmHelp: Exactly the number of ticked registrations — anything else erases nothing.
registrations.registrationsErased: {erased} registrations erased for good. {failed} could not be erased.

events.registrationModeTitle: The registration mode, from the event's settings
events.seriesRenewsUntil: Renews itself: the platform creates the dates {weeks} weeks ahead, until {until}.
events.seriesRenewsForever: Renews itself: the platform creates the dates {weeks} weeks ahead, for ever.
events.seriesDeleteNote: A series is deleted from the bar above the list: tick it, then “Delete the ticked ones”.
events.tableCaption: The club's events, with their status, date and number of registrations
events.bulkArchiveHelp: Archiving takes an event off the site without deleting anything. An event somebody else has edited in the meantime is not archived, so their change is not lost.
events.eventsArchived: {archived} events archived. {failed} could not be archived.
events.deleteBlocked: Cannot be deleted: {count} people have registered. Archive the event, or use “Permanent deletion…” below, which deletes the registrations too.
events.eventsRepeated: The series is running: {created} dates created now, up to {until} — the next eight weeks. The platform creates the rest by itself, always eight weeks ahead, until the chosen date or for ever; there is nothing more to press.
events.bulkHelp: Tick events in the list, or all of them. “Publish” sends them through review and publishes the ones complete in both languages — a whole series at once; “Archive” takes them off the site; “Delete” removes the ones nobody has registered for.
events.eventsDeleted: {deleted} events deleted. {failed} could not be deleted — they have registrations. Archive those, or use “Permanent deletion…” in the row's ⋮ menu, which deletes the registrations too.
events.eventsPublished: {published} events published. {failed} could not be (a language incomplete, or changed meanwhile).
events.eventErased: Event permanently deleted, together with {erased} registrations.

confirm.duplicateBody: A copy is created as a draft, with its own page addresses. It is not featured and it is not published.
confirm.deleteBody: Deleting is permanent. Only an event nobody has registered for can be deleted; for one that has happened, archive it instead.
confirm.bulkDeleteBody: Deleting is permanent. Every ticked event nobody has registered for is removed, in both languages; the ones with registrations are left as they are and counted.
confirm.archiveBody: The event comes off the site, in both languages. You can bring it back later by sending it through review and publishing it again.
confirm.removeTestBody: Every test registration for this event is deleted, along with the synthetic participants behind them. Real registrations are left untouched.
confirm.cancelRegistrationBody: The place is released immediately and offered to the first person on the waiting list. The registration itself is kept, marked cancelled.
confirm.repeatBody: The next events are created at the chosen interval, each with its own address. You can edit or delete them one by one afterwards.
confirm.bibsBody: Every confirmed registration without a number gets the next free one, in order of confirmation. Numbers already given stay.
confirm.bulkEraseTitle: Erase the ticked registrations for good?
confirm.bulkEraseBody: This cannot be undone. The places are released through the waiting list and the participants' data leave the record.

errors.PICTURE_IN_USE: The picture is used on a page, an event or in an album. Take it out of there first.
errors.NOTHING_SELECTED: You did not tick any registration.
errors.UNAUTHENTICATED: Your session has ended. Sign in again.
errors.FORBIDDEN: Your role does not allow this.
errors.VALIDATION_ERROR: Check what you entered; something is not valid.
errors.CONFLICT: Someone else saved while you were editing. Reload the page and reapply your changes — nothing of yours was overwritten.
errors.ERASE_NAME_MISMATCH: The name you typed is not this participant's name. Nothing was erased — type the name exactly as the row shows it.
errors.LEGAL_CONFIRMATION_MISMATCH: What you typed does not name this version. Nothing was deleted — type the phrase exactly as asked, for example “GDPR 2”.
errors.LEGAL_DELETE_NEEDS_REASON: Type a reason. It is the only thing left after the deletion.
errors.LEGAL_TERMS_IN_FORCE: This version of the terms has been in force, so it cannot be deleted: whoever registered in that window accepted it, and a registration does not record which version of the terms it was. You can withdraw it instead — it stays on the record and is offered to nobody.

editor.startsAtHelp: Local time of the event ({timezone}). For a race this is the gathering time.
editor.raceStartsAtHelp: When the gun goes, if that differs from the gathering time. Leave empty when there is only one time.
editor.mapUrlHelp: Optional. The meeting point on Google Maps or any other map. It must start with https://.
editor.locationHelp: The place, as you would tell a friend: a name, a street, or both. The shared name, filled in once; if the place goes by another name in English, write that one under “Content”, on the language's tab.
editor.locationNameInLanguageHelp: Optional. What the meeting point is called on this language's page — “Tractorul Park” on the English one, for instance. Leave it empty and the page uses the name from “{panel}”.
editor.featured: Lead the site with this event
editor.featuredHelp: Only one event can be featured. The previously featured one loses the flag automatically.
editor.specialHelp: An edition apart — an anniversary, a charity run, a race the club joins somebody else at. Shown with a badge on the card and on the page. Any number of events may be special, including one date of a series; the mark does not travel to the other dates.
editor.eventFieldsReadOnly: Only an editor or an administrator can change the times, the map link and the featured event.
editor.translationReadOnly: The words are the Redactor’s or the Administrator’s — yours are the Settings: the date, the place, the route, the places, the registrations and race day. Ask the Administrator to change anything here.
editor.saveCoversSettingsOnly: The save below covers the event’s settings. Nothing under “Content” is saved from here, because those words are not this role’s.
editor.liveWarning: This event is published. Your changes become public the moment you save.
editor.acknowledgeLive: I understand that I am editing published content.
editor.acknowledgeLiveHint: Tick that you understand you are changing published content to be able to save.
editor.slugHelp: The page address, in lowercase words joined by hyphens. It can only change before the first publication.
editor.slugLocked: The page has been published, so its address stays as it is.
editor.costHelp: Free text: "Free", "50 lei". Leave empty when no cost has been stated.

fields.title: Title
fields.excerpt: Summary — shown on the page, on the listing card and in shares
fields.checklist: What to bring (one line, in the emails and the calendar)
fields.body: Content — shown on the event page, under the title

editor.sharedFieldHelp: The same in both languages. Filled in once.
editor.contentHelp: The same event, in two languages. The words change here — and the place's name, when English calls it something else; the time, the map, the difficulty and the cost are below, once, shared by both.
editor.noTransitions: Your role cannot move this event from its current state.
editor.incompleteForPublication: Both languages must be complete before this event can be published. Missing: {detail}.
editor.newHelp: Both languages are filled in here, because an event goes live in both at once. The event is created as a draft; everything can still be changed afterwards on its own page.
editor.excerptHelp: One or two sentences: what the event page, the listing card (with a picture, if you put one in) and the shares carry. Required before publication.
editor.excerptEmpty: (required before publication — press to write it)
editor.scheduleHelp: The programme itself is the timed rows under “{panel}” → “{section}”, shared by both languages. Here you write, in this language, what does not fit a row — how the kit is collected, the cut-off rules. On the event page it appears beneath the rows; the reminder email repeats the rows and points here.
editor.programmeHelp: The day by the hour, one row each: kit pickup, the briefing, the start, the cut-offs, the awards. Shown as a list on the event page, repeated in the reminder email, and each row is its own entry in the calendar file. A row left empty is ignored. If you change the event's start date, the rows' dates move with it, and a new row starts on the event's day.
editor.programmeNotesHint: What does not fit a row — how the kit is collected, the cut-off rules — is written under “{panel}”, in each language, at “{fold}”; it appears on the page beneath these rows.
editor.rulesHelp: Optional. The race rules — what is allowed, what is not, how the kit is collected, the deadlines. Shown on the event page under “Rules”; the declaration and the emails point there.
editor.checklistHelp: Optional, at most 300 characters: “race number, water, a jacket”. It goes in the confirmation email, the reminder and the calendar entry.
editor.typeHelp: A group run is simply turned up to: no registration, no participants, no programme. A race has all of them; a hike, a coffee, an equipment test and another event may take registrations; an external event is somebody else's — its registration is on their page.
editor.timezoneHelp: The zone the times below are typed in. For Brașov, Europe/Bucharest.
editor.endsAtHelp: Optional. Leave empty when the club has stated only a start.
editor.registrationModeHelp: Registration here needs a declaration; registration elsewhere needs the organiser's link.
editor.capacityHelp: Leave empty for unlimited. It cannot be lowered below the places already taken.
editor.capacityWaiting: On the waiting list: {waiting}. If you raise the number, the new places are offered at once, in order, 24 h each.
editor.registrationWindowHelp: Leave the opening empty and registration opens when the event is published; leave the closing empty and it closes when the event starts.
editor.declarationDocumentHelp: Chosen from the approved versions. This text is never edited here — a new version arrives through a migration.
editor.declarationNone: No approved declaration exists in this environment, so no event can take registrations here yet.
editor.participantList: Publish the participant list on the event page
editor.participantListHelp: Publishes the names of the people who confirmed their registration and did not ask to be left out. No email addresses, and nothing about unconfirmed registrations. This is a disclosure of personal data: the approved privacy notice must describe it before this is switched on.
editor.externalHelp: Both only for an event registered elsewhere. The link must start with https://.
editor.deleteHelp: A duplicate is created as a draft, is never featured, and gets its own page addresses. Deleting is for an event nobody has registered for; archive the ones that happened.
editor.routeUrlHelp: Where the route can be seen — a Strava route or activity, or any other https:// link. Leave empty if there is not one.
editor.repeatHelp: Make this a standing series: the same details at a fixed interval, the time kept in the event's own zone, until a date or for ever. The next eight weeks are created now and the platform keeps creating the weeks that follow, each date its own event — cancel or move one without touching the rest. Each date gets an address with its day (“sunday-run-2026-10-04”). Dates are drafts unless you tick publish.
editor.repeatUntilHelp: Leave empty for a series without an end.
editor.repeatRuleForever: {sentence} — for ever. The next eight weeks are always created; the dates are in the list.
editor.repeatRuleUntil: {sentence} — until {until}. The dates are in the list.
editor.repeatStopHelp: No further dates are made; the ones that exist stay (tick them in the list to delete them).
editor.repeatStopped: The series is stopped: no further dates will be made.
editor.savedSeries: Saved — and on {applied} more dates of the series.
editor.savedSeriesOffered: Saved — and on {applied} more dates of the series; places offered to the waiting list: {offered}.
editor.savedOffered: Saved — places offered to the waiting list: {offered}.

scope.title: Save for:
scope.help: As in Google Calendar: only what you changed here reaches the other dates — a new time lands at that time on each date's own day; a date moved or cancelled on its own stays so unless the place or the status is what you changed. Each date's page address stays.
scope.chosen: this date and {count} more ticked above

editor.repeatOfNote: A save reaches every date of the series by default — the ticks above and the box by Save show exactly which. A cancellation, a different place or a different time stay here alone if you untick the others.

series.position: Date {position} of {count} in the series. Tick the dates the save should reach; the arrow opens a date.

editor.repeatPublish: Publish the editions as they are created (this event is published, so the copies are complete too).
editor.repeatWeekdaysHelp: This event's own day is always in the series; tick the others too — Wednesday, say, for a Sunday run. Only days after this event are made. Nothing ticked: the event's own day alone, at the chosen interval.
editor.repeatOnCreateHelp: Optional. Tick it and choose the interval: the dates of the next eight weeks are created with the event, and the platform creates the ones that follow by itself, always eight weeks ahead, until the chosen date or for ever. Each date is its own event with its day's address; they are drafts unless you tick publish.
editor.createdWithSeries: The event and {created} editions were created, as drafts. Tick them in the events list and publish them together.
editor.durationMinutesHelp: How long it lasts, in minutes — 90, say. The end is worked out from it. Leave empty if none was announced.
editor.coHostHelp: Optional. The organizations the club holds the event with — an NGO, a shop, a brand, another club — one per row, with their page if they have one. Shown as “Together with A, B, and C” on the page and on the card, and named as organizers after the club to Google. Partners travel to every date of a series.
editor.stravaEventUrlHelp: Optional. The event's address in the Strava club (strava.com/clubs/…/group_events/…), for those who RSVP there. A recurring Strava event keeps one address for every date, so the series inherits it from the source event; any one date can change its own.
editor.facebookEventUrlHelp: Optional. The event's address on Facebook (facebook.com/events/…), for those who say "Going" there. A Facebook event with several dates keeps one address, so the series inherits it from the source event; any one date can change its own.
editor.bodyHelp: The full description, with headings, lists and links — the day's programme, what to bring, where to park. It appears at the top of the event page, directly under the title; the short description stays on the card.
editor.confirmationOpensDaysBefore: Participation confirmation: asked how many days before
editor.confirmationWindowHelp: For events further away than the first number, whoever confirms their email keeps the place until the deadline and signs the declaration (= confirms participation) inside that window; at the first number they get the reminder email. Put 0 in the first to ask for the signature at once (30 minutes), as for the weekly runs — which are within a week anyway.

typeNotes.GROUP_RUN: Group run: people simply turn up — no registration, no participants, no programme.
typeNotes.RACE: Race: registration, a declaration, race numbers and a programme for the day.
typeNotes.HIKE: Hike: may take registrations and have a programme, when places are limited.
typeNotes.COFFEE: Coffee: may take registrations, to book the table. No programme.
typeNotes.GEAR_TEST: Gear test: may take registrations and have a programme.
typeNotes.MEETUP: Special event: the one-off, with a partner or for an occasion. May take registrations and have a programme.
typeNotes.EXTERNAL: External event: it is somebody else's, and registration happens on the organizer's own page.

editor.deleteBlockedByTest: Cannot be deleted: it has {count} registrations, all of them test data. Remove those first, under “Test registrations” above.
editor.bibsOnlyTest: Numbers are given to real, confirmed registrations only. Everything here is test data, which never gets a number — for a rehearsal, add a participant at the desk.
editor.bibStartNumberHelp: Usually 1. Use 100 or 500 to give each distance its own band — numbers are given in order of registration, counting up from here.

bibDesign.title: What the race number looks like
bibDesign.intro: What is printed on the bib, and how large. The same choices show in the preview on the “Numbers” page and on the A4 sheet you send to the printer.
bibDesign.headerImageSrc: A picture instead of the coloured band
bibDesign.headerImageSrcHelp: It runs the full width across the top. With one chosen, the band, the logo and the text on it are not printed — the picture is the header.
bibDesign.sponsorImageSrcHelp: Above the small print at the foot. Fitted without being stretched.
bibDesign.previewCaption: Preview — this is how it prints
bibDesign.previewAlt: The race number as it would look with the current choices, for a runner named “Nume Prenume”
bibDesign.previewNote: The pictures are the ones already uploaded (the “Pictures” page). The preview above changes at once; the “Numbers” page and the PDF follow a save.

editor.bibColourHelp: The band across the top of the printed number, the one carrying the club's logo and the race. “The club's colour” unless you want a specific one.

signIn.developmentOnly: Development identities, on a local machine and in tests only. These are not real people.

staff.title: Staff
staff.name: Name
staff.inviteHelp: This puts the address on the team list and emails them the invitation: who added them, with which role, and the sign-in link. The sign-in account is not created on its own — set the Zitadel key (To do → “Invite the team”, SETUP.md §37) and we create it with a password link; until then create it in the Zitadel console. Access begins at their first sign-in.
staff.inviteHelpSends: This adds the address to the list of who is staff, creates their sign-in account and emails them the invitation — who added them, as what, the sign-in link — and the link to choose a password. Then they sign in at /admin.
staff.inviteSent: Added. The invitation is on its way to their mailbox, with the link to choose a password.
staff.inviteExists: Added, the invitation is on its way. They already have a sign-in account with this address — they can sign in at /admin right away.
staff.inviteManual: Added, and the invitation is on its way. No sign-in account was created — the Zitadel key is not set. Create their account in the Zitadel console with exactly this address, or set the key (SETUP.md §37) and press “Resend the invitation”.
staff.inviteFailed: Added and the invitation is on its way, but the sign-in provider refused to create the account ({reason}). They can create it at the sign-in page with exactly this address.
staff.tableCaption: The accounts that may sign in to the backoffice, with each one's role
staff.empty: There is no staff account yet.
staff.resendInviteBody: An email goes to {email} with the sign-in link.
staff.passwordResetBody: Zitadel sends {email} a link to change their password. We never see the password.
staff.deactivateAccountBody: {name}'s account is switched off at the provider: they cannot sign in anywhere. The row in Echipa stays.
staff.revokeBody: {name} can no longer open the backoffice. The provider account stays — deactivate it separately if they are leaving the club.
staff.roleHelp: Each role can do what the one below it can, plus what it says here. Volunteers see the desk only.

roles.CONTRIBUTOR: the desk: scans codes, marks people present, confirms on paper, gives a free place, types a number. That is all.
roles.COPYWRITER: the words: descriptions, rules, programmes and the site's pages, in both languages. No settings, no publishing.
roles.MODERATOR: the events: creates, configures (dates, places, registration), publishes, the gallery.
roles.DEV: plus the technical page /devs. No participant data.
roles.ADMIN: plus registrations, the export, the legal texts, the emails, the tasks.
roles.SUPERADMIN: plus the team: who has access and with which role.

staff.resendFailed: The invitation did not go out: the identity provider has no account with this address ({reason}). Check the address in the table — if it is wrong, withdraw access and add the person again with the right one.
staff.passwordResetSent: Done. They have been emailed the link for setting a new password.
staff.accountDeactivated: The sign-in account is deactivated: they can no longer sign in anywhere. The team row stays — to take their access away too, use “Withdraw access”.
staff.accountReactivated: The sign-in account is active again.
staff.accountMissing: The identity provider has no account with this address, so there was nothing to change. Check the address in the table.
staff.accountUnconfigured: This needs the Zitadel key (To do → “Invite the team”, SETUP.md §37). Until then, from the Zitadel console.
staff.noAccountHelp: “No sign-in account”: the person is on the list, but Zitadel has no account with their address, so they cannot sign in — usually they were added while the invitation key could not create accounts. queue.title: The registration queue
queue.holdsHelp: “Held” are the places kept while somebody signs the declaration (30 minutes, or until the confirmation deadline for events more than a week away) or answers a waiting-list offer (24 hours). A hold past its deadline stays the person's — they can sign online any time, or on paper at the desk — and is released only when somebody is waiting for a place or the event starts. Free = places − confirmed − held, exactly the formula the public sees.
queue.lineEmpty: Nobody is waiting. The list fills once the places are gone.
queue.interestTitle: Addresses waiting for the opening notice: {count}
queue.interestHelp: Left at "Tell me" on the event's page. Each gets one email on the job's first run after registration opens and is deleted with it. If somebody writes that they no longer want the message, type their address here: it leaves the list. The addresses themselves are not shown.
queue.interestRemoved: The address was removed from the notification list.
queue.interestNotFound: That address was not on this event's list. Check whether they wrote from another one.
queue.simulate: How to simulate the waiting list (not in production): set a small number of places in Settings, save, then add more test registrations below than there are places — the first take the places (as 30-minute holds), the rest queue here, in order. Cancel a confirmed one, let a hold lapse (the maintenance job runs every 15 minutes) or raise the number of places and the first in line gets the offer; its email shows in the Outbox on that registration.

testRegistrations.title: Test registrations
testRegistrations.explanation: Synthetic participants on reserved @test.invalid addresses, which can never receive mail. They go through the ordinary submission and confirmation path, so they occupy places and fill the waiting list exactly as real people do — and they are left out of the CSV export and labelled everywhere they are listed. Not available in production.

legal.title: Legal documents
legal.intro: The three texts a participant accepts. An approved version never changes (people signed exactly that text); a correction is a new version.

legal.immutabilityNotice: An approved version is never edited and never deleted: participants signed exactly that text, and what the club published stays on the record. A correction is a new version. An unapproved draft can be deleted, because nobody has seen it.
legal.readOnlyNotice: This version is approved, so its text is fixed: participants have relied on it. To change the wording, start the next version from this one — it opens prefilled, you edit, save the draft, read it and approve it. The old version stays exactly as it was.

Written exactly so, with double braces.

legal.bodyHelp: A blank line separates paragraphs. A line starting with ## is a section heading. A link: [the words](https://…). A picture, on a line of its own: ![what it shows](https://…) — copy the address from Gallery → Pictures.
legal.keyLocked: The document cannot change after creation.
legal.editorWarning: This is the club’s legal text. Write or paste only wording the club has approved — never invent legal content.
legal.approveHelp: Once approved the text is public and can no longer be edited. A later correction means a new version.
legal.approveConfirm: I confirm the club has approved this text and it may become public
legal.legalVersionApproved: The version is approved and now public.

legal.deleteBody: The draft and its text in both languages go permanently. Nobody has seen it: a draft is never public and nobody has signed it.
legal.deleteBlockedApproved: Approved — cannot be deleted. What the club published stays on the record.
legal.deleteBlockedReferenced: Cannot be deleted: {signatures} signatures, {events} events and {acknowledgements} registrations depend on this version.
legal.newFromTemplateComplete: Prefilled with the platform's text and the club's facts, complete. Read it all, save the draft, then approve it from its page.

legal.withdrawBlockedCurrent: In force right now — it cannot be withdrawn. Approve its successor first; then this one can go.
legal.withdrawBlockedReferenced: Cannot be withdrawn: {signatures} signatures, {events} events and {acknowledgements} registrations depend on this version.
legal.withdrawnNotice: This version was withdrawn on {date}. Its text stays here, on the record, with its number, but it no longer appears publicly and can no longer be chosen on an event.

legal.removeBlockedReferenced: Can neither be withdrawn nor deleted: {signatures} signatures, {events} events and {acknowledgements} registrations depend on this version.
legal.removeBlockedCurrent: In force right now — it can neither be withdrawn nor deleted. Approve its successor first; then this one can go.
legal.deleteMeans: Deleting is permanent: the text goes entirely, and version number {version} stays retired for good.
legal.legalVersionErased: {phrase} has been deleted permanently. Its number stays retired: it will never be given to another version.

erase.title: Delete permanently: {document}, version {version}
erase.whatGoes: {document}, version {version}, in force since {date}, goes permanently: the text in both languages, the titles and the row itself. It cannot be recovered.
erase.numberRetired: Version number {version} stays retired for good. The next version of this document takes the next number, never {version} again, so a number people already ticked at registration can never end up on different words.
erase.auditOnly: One trace is left: an audit line with the document, the number, the date it took effect, who approved it, the SHA-256 of each language's text and the reason you type. The text itself is kept nowhere.
erase.nothingDepends: It can be deleted because nothing depends on it: no signature, no event, no registration — and it is not the text in force right now.
erase.alreadyWithdrawn: You already withdrew this version, on {date}. Deleting is the second and final step: now it leaves the record as well.
erase.notWithdrawn: This version has not been withdrawn. If you only want it to stop being offered anywhere, withdraw it from the list instead: it stays on the record, with its text and its number. Deleting cannot be undone.
erase.phraseHelp: Type exactly “{phrase}” to confirm. Anything else stops the deletion.
erase.reasonHelp: It stays in the audit log. It is the only thing that survives the deletion.
erase.blockedDraft: This is a draft, not an approved version. Delete it from the list with the button on its own row, with no typed confirmation: nobody has seen it and its number was never given to anyone.
erase.blockedReferenced: Cannot be deleted: {signatures} signatures, {events} events and {acknowledgements} registrations depend on this version. What people accepted stays.
erase.blockedCurrent: This is the version in force right now. Approve its successor first; then this one can be withdrawn or deleted.
erase.blockedTermsInForce: This version of the terms has been in force, so it cannot be deleted. Whoever registered in that window accepted it, and a registration does not record which version of the terms it was — so nobody can be shown not to have relied on it, and deletion destroys the words themselves. Withdrawal is what can be done: the version stays on the record, with its number, and is offered to nobody.

approveLegalText.title: Approve the legal text
approveLegalText.todo: A SAMPLE, unapproved text is on the site today. Until the club approves the privacy notice, the terms and the declaration, registration refuses everyone. The procedure is docs/RUNBOOKS.md § Legal document version.
approveLegalText.done: The club’s approved wording is published.
how: The short way (§132): /admin/legal → the “One step” box → check the legal name, CIF, seat and email shown → “Approve the three texts now”. Done: the notice, the terms and the declaration are in force, with the club's facts written in.
To read first: under the box, “start from the platform's text” → open each, read, then press the button in the box.
The long way, for a change: “New version” → text → save the draft → PDF → “Approve”. An approved text never changes; a correction is the next version.
On each event, under Registration, pick the approved declaration (if not already).

liveEmail.title: Email to real participants
liveEmail.todo: The sending domain {mailDomain} verified in Mailgun, then EMAIL_DELIVERY_MODE=live on production — the steps are below. Until then messages are either captured or reach at most 5 authorised addresses in the sandbox (allowlist). Mode right now
how: In Mailgun: Sending → Domains → “Add new domain”. Name: {mailDomain}. Region: EU. Not the main domain — that stays free for the club's own mailboxes.

Mailgun shows the DNS records to create: two TXT (SPF and DKIM) and one CNAME (tracking). Add them at ROMARG → cPanel → Zone Editor exactly as Mailgun shows them, with the short name (no repeated domain). Mind the DKIM one: the value is over 255 characters and cPanel cuts it — enter it as two quoted strings on one line (“k=rsa; p=…first part” “…the rest”), or Mailgun sees it truncated. Then “Verify” in Mailgun — up to an hour.

Still in Mailgun: Sending → API keys → a sending key (MAILGUN_API_KEY). Sending → Webhooks → copy the “HTTP webhook signing key” (MAILGUN_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_KEY) and add the webhook {webhookUrl} for “Permanent Failure” and “Spam Complaints” — the two the application acts on (a rejected address shows at the desk and on the registration). “Delivered” is optional.

In Vercel, the production project → Settings → Environment Variables (or `vercel env add NAME production`): MAILGUN_DOMAIN={mailDomain}, MAILGUN_API_KEY, MAILGUN_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_KEY, MAILGUN_API_BASE_URL=https://api.eu.mailgun.net/v3, EMAIL_REPLY_TO=a mailbox the club reads (if none exists yet, leave the variable unset — an empty one is refused at startup). The sender is “Brașov Runners” <noreply@{mailDomain}> with no further setting.

Rehearse on QA, not on production (production refuses registrations until the legal texts are approved): on the QA Vercel project set the same MAILGUN_DOMAIN, MAILGUN_API_KEY, MAILGUN_API_BASE_URL (the mode stays allowlist, EMAIL_ALLOWLIST=your address), redeploy, register on QA — the email comes from noreply@{mailDomain}. When it does: on production EMAIL_DELIVERY_MODE=live, redeploy. This row turns green.

scheduler.title: Production monitors on cron-job.org
scheduler.todo: Monitors for the two scheduled jobs (email-outbox and registration-maintenance), with this environment’s JOB_SECRET — SETUP.md §26: every 15 minutes by day (07–23, Romania time) and hourly at night. Email goes out right after each registration anyway; the monitors expire held places and retry what failed. Missing or late
scheduler.done: Both jobs are running on time.
how: On cron-job.org (free account): Settings → Time zone = Europe/Bucharest. Then “Create cronjob”, four times for production: two per address (one for the day, one for the night).

The addresses: {outboxUrl} and {maintenanceUrl}. On all of them: Request method POST, and under Headers: Authorization = Bearer followed by this environment's JOB_SECRET (the value in Vercel → Settings → Environment Variables; it is not shown here).

Day: Execution schedule → Custom → every day, hours 7–22, minutes 0, 15, 30, 45. Night: Custom → every day, hours 23, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, minute 0. Not every 5 minutes: the Neon database would never sleep — on Free the included hours would run out mid-month with the site down until the next month; on Launch every awake hour is paid for.

Turn on email notification on failure, so a dead monitor tells you. This row turns green on the first run; /devs shows each job with its last run, and the database's consumption. At night the site answers its first request more slowly — that is intended.
On QA: one pair only, every 60 minutes day and night (or paused when not testing): QA spends its own project's hours too — included on Free, paid on Launch.

The third monitor, the one that tells you when emails stop going out: “Create cronjob” with the address {baseUrl}/api/health, Request method GET, no header, every 30 minutes (Custom → every day, every hour, minutes 0 and 30). Under Notifications tick “on failure” (and “when the job gets disabled”). The page answers 503 while a message is deferred by the daily allowance, has failed, or was left unpicked by the monitors — and cron-job.org emails you from its own mail, not through Mailgun. When it clears, it answers 200 again and you get “job successful”.

inviteStaff.title: Invite the team
inviteStaff.todo: There is a single staff account — the one inserted by hand. From /admin/staff an Administrator invites organizers by email address; their Zitadel account is bound on first sign-in.
how: Open /admin/staff, type the person's email address and pick the role: Moderator (writes and publishes), Administrator (registrations, legal texts, this page) or Superadministrator (the team too).

“Add” emails them the club's invitation: who added them, as what, the sign-in link. With the invitation key set (SETUP.md §37: a Zitadel service user's token as ZITADEL_MANAGEMENT_PAT on both Vercel projects), it also creates their Zitadel account and they get the link to choose a password too. Without it, the person creates their account at the sign-in page with exactly that address. Zitadel only proves who they are; the list here decides whether they are staff.
They open {baseUrl}/admin, sign in through Zitadel, done. “Access Denied” means an unverified email or a different address from the invited one.

inviteKey.title: The invitation key (Zitadel)
inviteKey.todo: The key is missing (ZITADEL_MANAGEMENT_PAT). Without it, “Add” on Echipa puts the person on the list and sends our invitation, but creates no sign-in account — and the sign-in page has no “create an account”, so the person is stuck. The key is a Zitadel service user's token with the Org User Manager role, set on both Vercel projects (SETUP.md §37).
inviteKey.blind: The key is set and authenticates, but can do nothing: asked which accounts it sees, Zitadel shows it not even yours — though you are signed in with it right now. The service user is not an “Org User Manager” of the organization. Every “Add” on Echipa writes the row and creates no account, and the colleague meets “User not found in the system” at sign-in (DECISIONS.md §288).
inviteKey.refused: The key is set, but Zitadel refuses the account search every “Add” makes — usually the token was revoked, or the service user is not an “Org User Manager” of the organization. Zitadel's answer
inviteKey.unreachable: The key could not be checked: Zitadel did not answer. Not necessarily a problem with the key — reload the page in a few minutes. The answer
inviteKey.done: The key works: checked just now with a real search, it found your account. “Add” on Echipa creates the sign-in account and Zitadel sends the password link.
how: Zitadel console → Users → Service Accounts → New: user name “brasovrunners-invites”, name “Brașov Runners — invitații”, access token type Bearer. Create.

Organization → Managers → + New: the service account, role Org User Manager (it may create users and send their invitation codes; nothing else). The dialog is called “Add an Administrator” and names the service user at the top; if it asks for a Loginname, that is “brasovrunners-invites”. Careful: “Role Assignments” is NOT this — that page grants roles inside a project and has nothing to do with managing users; a service account can sit there Active, looking configured, and still be unable to create anybody (DECISIONS.md §288).

On the service account → Personal Access Tokens → New. The console offers no expiry here and the token does not expire — it is a secret that has to be revoked by hand, on the same screen, when it is no longer wanted. Copy it (shown once) into the password manager and note there that it has no end date.
Vercel → the production project → Settings → Environment Variables: ZITADEL_MANAGEMENT_PAT = the token (Production). The same on the QA project. Redeploy both.

Check: reload this page after the redeploy — the row turns green when the key finds your account, without inviting anybody. Then, on Echipa, “Add” creates the account and Zitadel sends the password link; whoever has not signed in yet has “Resend the invitation” on their row.
howBroken: Zitadel console → Organization → Managers → + New: pick the key's service account (SETUP.md §37: “brasovrunners-invites”), role Org User Manager — it may create users and send their invitation codes, nothing else. The dialog is called “Add an Administrator”; if it asks for a Loginname, that is the service account's name.

Not “Role Assignments”: that page grants roles inside a project and has nothing to do with managing users. A service account can sit there Active, looking perfectly configured, and still be unable to create anybody — exactly what happened on the club's own instance (DECISIONS.md §288).

If Zitadel answered 401 or the token was revoked: on the service account → Personal Access Tokens → New, then the new token as ZITADEL_MANAGEMENT_PAT on both Vercel projects and redeploy (SETUP.md §37, steps 3–4).

Check: reload this page. The row turns green when the key finds your account — without inviting anybody. Then Echipa: every colleague marked “No sign-in account” was added while the key could not create accounts — ⋮ → “Revoke access”, then “Add” again with the same address; this time the account is created and Zitadel sends them the password link.
howUnreachable: Reload the page in a few minutes: the check runs on every open, with a single request to Zitadel.

If it stays so, open the Zitadel console: if that does not open either, the provider has a problem and there is nothing to do here; if it does, check on the service account that the token exists and, on Vercel, that ZITADEL_MANAGEMENT_PAT and AUTH_ZITADEL_ISSUER are set on this project (SETUP.md §37).

mediaStorage.title: Photo storage (Cloudflare R2)
mediaStorage.todo: The gallery needs somewhere to put photos. Until it is configured, albums can be created but cannot receive photos. Free at the club's size; Cloudflare still asks for a card on the account to enable R2.
how: A Cloudflare account (free) on the club's address. The domain does not move there.
Left menu → R2 Object Storage → enable R2 (this is where the card is asked for; nothing is charged under 10 GB).

Create bucket → name “brasovrunners-media”, location “European Union”. Then, in the bucket's settings, enable “Public access” through the r2.dev subdomain (or a custom domain) and copy the public address — that is R2_PUBLIC_BASE_URL.

R2 → “Manage R2 API Tokens” → Create API token → name “brasovrunners-site”, permission “Object Read & Write”, this bucket only. Copy the Access Key ID, the Secret Access Key and the S3 endpoint (shown once).

In Vercel → the production project (and QA) → Settings → Environment Variables: R2_ENDPOINT, R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID, R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, R2_BUCKET=brasovrunners-media, R2_PUBLIC_BASE_URL. Redeploy. This row turns green and the album page gets its upload button.

tasks.servicesTitle: The services, one at a time
tasks.servicesIntro: One row for each service the site depends on: the plan we are on, what it costs today, what we get for free, the limit we will meet first, how close we are right now, what happens when we cross it, and what the next step up costs.

domain.name: The site's address (the .com domain)

mailgun.name: Mailgun (sending email)
mailgun.freeGives: Free: 100 emails a day — on one Mailgun account, used by both QA and production: what one sends comes off what the other can still send. Until the club has its own address, email can only go to five test addresses.
mailgun.ceiling: The first limit: 100 emails a day, which is about 33 entries, because one complete entry takes three emails.
mailgun.whenCrossed: Emails over the limit are not lost: they wait in the queue and go out after midnight. But a race whose confirmations only arrive the next morning is a bad race, so the paid plan is bought before entries open, not during them.
mailgun.closeMeasured: {used} of {of} emails have gone out today — enough left for about {left} entries. Counted from this environment's own messages; the allowance belongs to one Mailgun account, shared with the other environment.
mailgun.bumpBack: Taken for the month of the race and stopped the month after. One month per race, not a long-term subscription.

vercel.name: Vercel (where the site lives)
vercel.freeGives: Free: enough traffic and power for a club site, but only for non-commercial use.
vercel.ceiling: The first limit: the free plan requires that the site is not used commercially. The club sells nothing and takes no money, so we are fine.
vercel.whenCrossed: An event asking for a compulsory fee would count as commercial; a donation would not — they say so themselves. There is one more thing, and it has nothing to do with the club: if anybody is ever paid to work on this site, that counts as commercial too. And one more to know: if a limit on the free plan is exceeded, the feature stops for 30 days and you cannot pay to restart it — which is why you move up before a race, not during one.
vercel.closeYes: A published event is marked as charging a fee — check how it is worded.
vercel.closeNo: No published event asks for money.
vercel.bumpBack: This one does not come back down: it is not a busy weekend, it is a change in how the site is used. Unless it was taken purely for traffic.

neon.name: Neon (the database)
neon.freeGives: Free: a small database (half a gigabyte) and an amount of work included every month.
neon.ceiling: The first limit: the space and the monthly amount of work included.
neon.whenCrossed: On the free plan the database goes to sleep when nobody is using it, so the first page after a quiet spell is slow to load. Past the limit the site gets slow and errors can appear. The next step up is paid by usage, not as a fixed subscription.
neon.closeMeasured: Measured from the database: {used} MB of {of} MB used. Compute hours (CU) are on /devs.
neon.monthly: Monthly cost if we left Free, at this month's pace ({cu} CU-hours so far): about ${usd}/month on Launch (${rate}/CU-hour, ${storageRate}/GB, no subscription).
neon.monthlyUnknown: Monthly cost on Launch: ${rate}/CU-hour + ${storageRate}/GB, no subscription. The exact pace appears once NEON_API_KEY is set.
neon.closeUnknown: Not measured: the site does not know how much has been used. It is visible in the Neon account and worth a look before a race.
neon.closeNo: No ceiling on Launch: what is used is what is paid.
neon.bumpBack: Taken for the days entries are open and dropped once they close.

launch.freeGives: Launch: paid by usage, no subscription — compute hours and storage are billed at the plan's rates. The Free plan remains the way back, at the December review.
launch.ceiling: No ceiling: nothing stops when usage grows — the bill grows.
launch.whenCrossed: What keeps the bill small is what kept Free alive: the database sleeps after five minutes without a request, and the monitors wake it every 15 minutes by day and once an hour at night. A monitor every 5 minutes would keep it awake around the clock and turn sleeping hours into paid ones.
launch.close: No ceiling. This month, at the pace so far ({cu} CU-hours, about {perDay} CU-hours a day): about ${usd} a month (${rate}/CU-hour, ${storageRate}/GB-month) — an estimate; the invoice is Neon's.
launch.closeUnknown: No ceiling. The month's pace appears once NEON_API_KEY is set; until then the figure is in the Neon console → Billing (${rate}/CU-hour, ${storageRate}/GB-month).
launch.bumpBack: The way back is the December 2026 review: after real invoices, the club may choose Free again — one choice under “The Neon plan” on this page, no deployment; check Free's limits at that time on both projects first.

zitadel.freeGives: Free: up to 100 sign-ins a day and a single administrator of the Zitadel account. Signing in happens on the provider's address, not the club's — decided, not pending: a login address of our own would cost 100 USD a month.
zitadel.ceiling: The one limit that matters: a single administrator of the Zitadel account. If that person is unavailable, nobody can invite anybody.

desk.title: Number pickup desk
desk.howTitle: How race day works, step by step
how: Before the race (organizer): on the event page, under “Race numbers”, press “Assign numbers”, then “Download the sheet (PDF)” and print it. Print the approved declaration too (Legal documents → PDF), a few copies, for anyone who signs on the spot.

Volunteers: invite them from “Staff” with the Volunteer role. With their account they open this page on their phone. That is all they see: name, state, number. No email addresses, and nobody can be cancelled from here.

Every confirmed participant got a QR code by email. At the desk: press “Scan” (on Android) or open the phone's camera and point it at the code — the person's page opens. Or search by name or by race number.
Press “Here” and hand over the number from the sheet. No number? Type it in the box and press “Save”.
No email arrived, or they cannot find the QR: search by name. If it says “pending”, give them the paper declaration to sign, press “Confirm here”, then “Here”.

Never registered at all: “Add somebody” — name and email; the “is at the desk” tick is already set. They sign the paper declaration, then “Here”. If the event is full they join the waiting list; “Give a place” only works once one is free.
Made a mistake? “Undo” takes it back. Every press stays in the registration's history, with your name on it.
At the end, the figures on this page are the race's figures: how many confirmed, how many here. Whoever did not come stays without “here”.

guide.title: How to use the platform
guide.intro: Who does what, step by step. Each section says which role it needs; yours is shown at the top next to your name. If a button is missing, you do not have the role for it — ask a superadministrator.

sections.title: Volunteer at the number pickup desk
sections.who: Role: Volunteer (or any role). On a phone.
steps: Open the site and press “Sign in” (at the bottom, or at /admin). Use the account the organizer gave you.
Press “Race day” in the top bar. Pick today's event from the list.
The participant shows the QR code from their email. Press “Scan” (Android) or open the phone's Camera app, point it at the code and tap the link that appears — the person's page opens.
Check the name, press “Here” and hand over the race number from the sheet (the number is shown large, left of the name).
No QR, or they cannot find the email: type part of the name in the search box and press “Search”. Same page, same buttons.
It says “pending” or “unconfirmed”: give them the paper declaration, they sign it, you press “Confirm here”, then “Here”.
No number: type it in the box and press “Save”. A number already given to somebody else is refused.

Never registered: press “Add somebody”, fill in name and email, “Add registration”. They sign the paper declaration, then “Here”. If the event is full they join the waiting list — “Give a place” only works once somebody withdrew.
Pressed the wrong thing: “Undo”. Everything you press stays in the history with your name — nothing is lost.
What you cannot do from here (and that is fine): cancel or erase registrations, see email addresses, export lists. For those, call an administrator.

sections.title: Participant — what it looks like from their side
steps: They register from the event page and get a verification email; they press the link and the place is held (30 minutes, or until the confirmation deadline for an event more than a week away). The deadline applies only if somebody is waiting for a place by then; otherwise the place stays theirs until the start.

They read and sign the declaration online, typing their name — or on paper, at the desk, on race day, before picking up their number. The registration becomes “confirmed” and they get the confirmation email with the QR code.
The same email has a “Manage your registration” link: from there they can withdraw, see their code and, from the day before the start, press “I have arrived”.
Event full: they join the waiting list and get an email when a place frees up, with 24 hours to sign the declaration.
No email arrived: on “Did not get the email?” (/registrations/resend) they ask for the link again. Or they come to the desk and a volunteer confirms them on the spot.

In their calendar: every event has “Google Calendar” and “Add to calendar (.ics)”; on the events page, “Subscribe” puts the club's whole calendar on the phone and it updates by itself when you publish something new.

sections.title: Copywriter — the events' texts and the pages
sections.who: Role: Copywriter. You write; you do not configure or publish.
steps: “Events” → pick the event → the Romanian tab and the English tab: the title, the short description, the description, the rules, the programme and the SEO fields. One save writes both languages.
A published event: what you save is on the site at once — tick “I know I am changing a published page”. The page's address does not change after publication.

A YouTube film: in the editor, the “YouTube” button → paste the film's address → “Add the film”. Click the film to give it a caption. On the page it appears closed, “Watch the film”; it loads only when the reader presses.
“Pages”: the site's standing pages. Create a draft, write in the editor (headings, lists, links, pictures), submit it for review; the Administrator publishes it.
Not yours, and not needed: the event's settings (date, places, registration), publishing, the gallery, the registrations. If a text depends on a wrong setting, tell the Organizer.
Both languages count: an event cannot be published without complete text in Romanian and in English, and the English page keeps its old text until you correct that too.

sections.title: Organizer — events and numbers
steps: The Administrator creates the event (“New event”, “Duplicate”, “Repeat”). You open it from “Events” and look after the Settings: the type, the date, the gun time, the duration, the meeting point, the address, the map link, the distance, the route, the difficulty, the cost.

Registrations: in Settings choose “Local registration”, set the capacity and the window, the participation window (how many days before a confirmation is asked, and when it expires), the bib band and the approved declaration.

The words — the title, the summary, the description, the rules, the programme — are the Redactor's or the Administrator's. You can read them and cannot save them; if a text is wrong, tell the Administrator.

Publishing: you press “Submit for review”. “Publish” is the Administrator's, as are taking a live event down and archiving one. Both languages go live together; an incomplete language blocks publishing.

Registrations (Organizer, not Tehnic): you see the whole list, each registration with its history, the export (Excel or CSV), the race numbers and the signed declarations. You cannot cancel, erase, rename or resend an email — those are the Administrator's.

Race numbers: “Assign numbers”, on the event page, is the Administrator's. The sheet is yours to download: “Download the sheet (PDF)” — two per A4, with the logo — from the event page or from “Registrations”. Print the declaration too (Legal documents → PDF) for on-the-spot signatures.
On race day: “Number pickup desk” from the event page, or “Race day” in the bar. The “Confirmed / Here” figures are the race's figures.

Race numbers: at confirmation everyone gets one at random. A preferential number: the registration's page → “Race number” — the free numbers are listed beside the field, type one, save; the participant gets the number by email, with the QR code. A number somebody else already wears is refused.
Afterwards: archiving a published event is the Administrator's. The photos are yours: “Gallery” — new album, upload from the phone, publish.

sections.title: Administrator — registrations, legal texts, staff
steps: “Registrations”: the full list, filters, name search, CSV export, each registration's page with its history. From there: correct a name, cancel (the place is released), erase on request, resend the email.
“Legal documents”: privacy notice, terms, declaration. New version → save the draft → PDF to review → “Approve”. An approved text never changes; a correction is the next version.

“Staff” (Superadministrator): add people by email and role. “Add” also creates their sign-in account and sends them the invitation to choose a password — you no longer go into Zitadel. If somebody does not get it, “Resend the invitation” on their row.

Volunteer accounts: in “Staff”, “Add” with the Volunteer role — the account and the invitation go out from there. One account per volunteer, so the history says who pressed; if there is no time, one shared “Desk volunteer” account works — the history will say “Desk volunteer”.
“To do”: what is still missing for the platform to take real registrations, read from the system, with the steps to follow.
“Configuration” (/devs): job status, which variables are set, database consumption, the theme lab.

“Emails” → “The Mailgun plan”: tell the platform which plan the Mailgun account is on. On Free, 100 messages a day go out (≈ 20 registrations); when you pay for a month of Basic before a race, pick Basic here and the figures on “Tasks” and the “Send now” button follow it; when you cancel, put Free back.

“To do” → “Costs” → “The Neon plan”: tell the platform which plan the Neon account is on — Free (hours and storage included, a stop when they run out) or Launch (by usage, chosen on 22 September 2026). /devs and the Neon row in the costs follow it, on each environment separately; the December review is the same choice, with no deployment.

sections.title: Declarations of own responsibility and personal data (GDPR)
sections.who: Role: Administrator. Read once, before the first event with registrations.
steps: The declaration's text is a legal document under “Legal documents”. Start from the platform's text (the “Declaration” link under “New version”): it is the club's declaration with its blanks as tokens — {{participant}}, {{idDocument}}, {{event}}, {{eventDate}}, {{eventLocation}}, {{signedAt}} — filled in automatically for each person and event. One approved text serves every event.

When signing, the participant reads the text filled in with their name and the event, types the series and number of their identity document (no photo or scan of an ID is ever uploaded) and writes their name as the signature. Recorded: the name, the document, the text's version, its fingerprint (SHA-256), the moment and the method. That is a simple electronic signature (eIDAS and Law 214/2024).

Right after signing, the participant receives the signed declaration by email as an attached PDF (“Your signed declaration”), plus a link to it from their registration page. At the desk, the kit is handed out against the identity document written in the declaration — it shows on the “Race day” row and in the CSV.

Whoever cannot sign from the email signs on paper: on the event page, “Paper declaration form (PDF)” prints the form with the event filled in. At the desk, “Confirm on paper” records the signature under the volunteer's name; the club keeps the signed original.

Where the declarations live: in the database (Neon, Frankfurt), as records — not as files. The PDF is generated from them on request, any time, identically. After the event, from the event page: “Signed declarations (PDF)” — all in one file, one per page (200 declarations ≈ 2 MB, a few seconds) — and the CSV export. Keep them in the club's own archive, with restricted access (they carry names and identity documents).

How long they are kept: registrations and declarations 3 years from the event (the general limitation period), then deleted automatically; earlier on request, with “Erase” on the registration page. Sent emails 90 days, spent links 30 days. The privacy notice says exactly this.

The privacy notice and the terms: start from the platform's text too — they are complete (GDPR art. 13, Law 190/2018, the processors, the periods, the rights, the ANSPDCP); you only fill in the legal name, the registered address, the registration number and the contact email, read, save the draft and approve. Without approved texts nobody can register.
The public display name (nickname) is off by default (FEATURE_DISPLAY_NAME): the list and the export show real names, and the kit is collected against an identity document.

Minors: a participant under 18 is registered by the parent/guardian, who types their name in the form's “Registering a minor” section (required under 18), signs the declaration with their own identity document and collects the kit; the desk and the export show “Minor — parent/guardian: <name>”.

staffProvider.title: Staff sign-in
staffProvider.body: Through the identity provider. Who may in is still decided by the staff_users table, not by the provider.

staffDevSwitcher.title: Staff sign-in
staffDevSwitcher.body: Development identities, local and test only. Not real people.

staffDisabled.title: Staff sign-in
staffDisabled.body: There is no way in at all: every staff route answers 404. Correct for an environment with no provider configured.

jobs.title: Scheduled jobs
jobs.body: The only thing that drains the email queue and expires holds. Without JOB_SECRET the endpoints refuse every caller, and the symptom is not an error — it is email that never arrives.

webhook.title: Mailgun webhook
webhook.body: How a bounce reaches the registration it belongs to. Without the signing key, requests are refused and delivery state stays unknown.

contactFormCapture.title: Contact form
contactFormCapture.body: Messages are kept in memory and go nowhere — the only mode locally and in tests; no SMTP connection is ever opened.

contactFormSmtp.title: Contact form
contactFormSmtp.body: Sends over SMTP, straight from the club's Gmail — not through Mailgun and not through the email queue. The recipients come from /admin/emails, or from CONTACT_FORM_TO while nobody is set there; the label beside this says which one answered.

contactFormNoRecipients.title: Contact form
contactFormNoRecipients.body: It can send, but there is nobody to send to: neither the list on /admin/emails nor CONTACT_FORM_TO holds an address. The “Write to us” page shows the club's address until somebody writes a recipient on /admin/emails — no redeploy needed.

contactFormOff.title: Contact form
contactFormOff.body: The “Write to us” page shows the club's address instead of the form. The sending account is missing: CONTACT_SMTP_USER (the Gmail address) and CONTACT_SMTP_PASSWORD (the app password). The recipients are written in the app, on /admin/emails; CONTACT_FORM_TO is only the fallback.

Devs.rateLimitsIntro: How many attempts each guarded action accepts in a fixed window, per key — an email identity, a registration, one email link, or one job. A limit somebody is hitting looks like "the site is broken" without anything being broken.
Devs.rolesIntro: Each role can do everything the one below it can, plus one thing more. The line that matters is between Technical and Admin: from there up, participant data is visible.

roleSummary.CONTRIBUTOR: the race-number desk, and nothing else
roleSummary.COPYWRITER: the words of any event and of the pages; submits for approval
roleSummary.MODERATOR: creates and configures events, publishes, the gallery
roleSummary.DEV: plus the configuration page. No participant data
roleSummary.ADMIN: plus registrations, participants, export, legal texts, deleting an event
roleSummary.SUPERADMIN: plus team administration: who has access and what they can do

Devs.emailVolumeIntro: Three messages per completed registration, against the provider's daily allowance. Check this before opening a registration window, not after. Counted from midnight UTC.

APP_ENV.what: Which deployment this is. It — not NODE_ENV — decides every environment-dependent rule: whether live email may be sent, whether the development sign-in switcher is permitted, and whether sample legal text and test registrations may exist at all.

values.local: A developer's own machine. Email is captured and never transmitted; the sign-in switcher is available; sample legal text is seeded.
values.test: The automated suites. Same guarantees as local, and nothing here ever reaches a person.
values.qa: The shared deployment colleagues try things on. Real database, real sign-in, and email either captured or restricted to an allowlist — never open delivery.
values.production: The club's real site. The only environment permitted to send live email, and the only one that refuses sample legal text and test registrations outright.

EMAIL_DELIVERY_MODE.what: How far a message actually goes once the outbox renders it. This is the guard between a test system and a stranger's inbox, and startup refuses any combination that would cross it.

values.capture: Nothing is transmitted. Messages are held in memory — which on a deployed serverless host means they reach nobody at all, so registration looks broken to anyone but a developer.
values.allowlist: Real delivery, but only to the addresses in EMAIL_ALLOWLIST; everything else is captured. This is what a Mailgun sandbox domain is, and it is how a small closed group tests the whole journey safely.
values.live: Real delivery to whoever registered. Permitted only when APP_ENV is production; stating it anywhere else fails at startup.

STAFF_AUTH_MODE.what: How a member of staff proves who they are. Participants never sign in at all — this is the backoffice door only, and the staff_users table decides who may come through it regardless of which mode is set.

values.dev-switcher: A local shortcut that lets a developer become any role without an identity provider. Permitted only when APP_ENV is local or test; stating it elsewhere fails at startup.
values.provider: The real thing: Auth.js with Zitadel. The provider proves the address, and the staff_users allowlist decides whether that address may in.
values.disabled: There is no way in. Every staff route answers 404 rather than a refusal, so the backoffice is unreachable rather than merely hidden. This is the correct setting for any environment with no identity provider configured.

Devs.operationalTitle: What each limit does when it is met
Devs.operationalIntro: Who stops you — the provider's own API, or this application's code — what the application does at that moment, and which variable or monitor is involved. Costs and plans are not here: they live on /admin/tasks, for the people who pay the invoice.

mailgunDaily.title: Mailgun's daily allowance (100 messages on the free plan)
mailgunDaily.body: Mailgun refuses the send with the same HTTP 400 it uses for a malformed message. The adapter recognises the limit wording, classifies the refusal as throttled, and the outbox row stays PENDING with its next attempt scheduled just after midnight UTC — not the ordinary backoff, which would spend all six attempts within an hour and mark a good message FAILED. The signal is the email-volume figure above; there is no configuration variable for the cap.

captureOnServerless.title: Capture mode delivers nothing on a deployed environment
captureOnServerless.body: The capture adapter holds messages in the process's memory, and on serverless hosting the process is gone before anybody could read the link. A colleague who is not on the allowlist registers and then simply never hears anything. Allowlist mode with a real provider is the only way somebody outside the code completes a registration.

schedulerFloor.title: The cadence of the scheduled jobs
schedulerFloor.body: Vercel Hobby allows one run a day and refuses a finer expression at deploy time, so the scheduler is the GitHub Actions workflow plus an external pinger; GitHub's own minimum is five minutes, and measured here the real cadence is roughly two hours. The application does not break in between: hold expiry is evaluated inside every capacity transaction (§10.6), so a late run delays a message rather than overbooking an event. Both endpoints are guarded by JOB_SECRET, and each job's liveness is reported below and in /api/health.

hobbyCapPause.title: Exceeding a Hobby cap pauses the feature for 30 days
hobbyCapPause.body: Not a bill — an outage with a fixed sentence, and you cannot buy your way out of it during the window. There is nothing the application can do at that point; the only response is to upgrade before the window. It is visible only in the Vercel dashboard — nothing here reports it.

identityDomain.title: Zitadel Free: zero custom domains, one administrator
identityDomain.body: No effect on the code, but it decides which host staff sign in on. While STAFF_AUTH_MODE=provider runs on the provider's hostname the limit is not felt; on the club's own domain it needs a paid tier. STAFF_AUTH_MODE=disabled answers 404 to every staff route, which is what an environment with no tenant should do.

statementTimeout.title: statement_timeout 10s and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout 30s
statementTimeout.body: Enforced by this application rather than by Neon: db/client.ts sets both on the pool. The risk was never the connection count (max: 10 is per warm instance, and PgBouncer accepts far more) but one unbounded query holding a Vercel function for 300 seconds. The first timeout is enforced by PostgreSQL, so it holds even when the Node process is frozen; the second covers an instance killed between two statements of an open transaction. There is no connection timeout, deliberately: on Neon Free the first request after an idle period waits for the database to wake.
